Senses.PreferredTarget: not blind to cause and effect
AlternateTargets: not ignorant of cause and effect
SearchAliases: not blind to cause and effect
not ignorant of cause and effect
Senses.Explanation: Not blind to cause and effect, or not obscuring cause and effect. The phrase occurs 150 times in 81 allowed texts, almost exactly alongside 'not falling into cause and effect' (不落因果, 151); the paired form 'not falling, not being blind' (不落不昧) occurs 86 times. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly contrasts the two phrases, while an unnamed monk inside the same commentary objects that even with 'not being blind to cause and effect' the fox body has not yet been shed. Dahui Zonggao preserves the paired questions but answers only by telling the questioner to raise them this way to people. Wumen Huikai asks why 'not falling' brought the fox body and why 'not being blind' shed it, then calls the pair 'two throws, one game' (不落不昧，兩采一賽). Chaozong Tongren rebukes both rejecting 'not falling' and clinging to 'not being blind' as tying oneself without a rope, yet continues by affirming 'not being blind to cause and effect' in his own stated frame. Later records continue asking whether the pair is the same or different. The records preserve competing deployments and questions; this entry does not select a winner among them.
Senses.Note: The primary sense is the shared phrase in the historical Baizhang public case, not a Baizhang-specific meaning. The fox-body sequence is translated because the record literally states it; no broader account is inferred from it. Wansong's contrast, the embedded monk's objection, Wumen's paired verdict, Chaozong's no-rope rebuke, and later same-or-different questions are preserved as speaker-owned positions. They do not create different referents and therefore do not justify a sense split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老人曰。大修行人還落因果也無。師曰。不昧因果。老人於言下大悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Meeting the Source (五燈會元), spoken by Baizhang Huaihai in his explicit section: the old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect; Baizhang answers 'not blind to cause and effect.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 不落因果是撥無斷見。不昧因果。是隨流得妙。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong Xingxiu writes in Wansong Elder's Commentary on Tiantong's Book of Serenity (萬松老人評唱天童覺和尚頌古從容庵錄), case eight, ‘Baizhang's fox’: Wansong explicitly contrasts the two phrases; this token belongs to the commentator, not to Baizhang's original exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一僧曰。只如不昧因果。也未脫得野狐身。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong Elder's Commentary on Tiantong's Book of Serenity (萬松老人評唱天童覺和尚頌古從容庵錄): an unnamed monk in Wansong Xingxiu's embedded report objects that even with ‘not being blind to cause and effect,’ the fox body has still not been shed. The unnamed monk, not Wansong, speaks the exact token.

Occurrences.Kwic: 前百丈云。不落因果。為甚麼墮野狐身。師云。逢人但恁麼舉。進云。只如後百丈道不昧因果。為甚麼脫野狐身。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue (大慧普覺禪師語錄): an unnamed monk asks why the later Baizhang's ‘not being blind to cause and effect’ shed the fox body. Dahui Zonggao answers without repeating the headword; he is respondent and record owner, not exact token speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問不落因果為甚麼墮野狐身。師曰。廬山五老峯。曰不昧因果為甚麼脫野狐身。師曰。南嶽三生藏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp (續傳燈錄), Yuquan Zonglian section: an unnamed monk asks why ‘not being blind to cause and effect’ shed the fox body. Yuquan answers with Nanyue's Three-Life Treasury without repeating the headword; he is respondent and section subject, not exact token speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不落因果。為甚墮野狐。不昧因果。為甚脫野狐。若向者裏著得一隻眼。便知得。前百丈贏得。風流五百生。頌曰。不落不昧兩采一賽不昧不落千錯萬錯
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's Barrier (無門關), written by Wumen Huikai: Wumen asks why 'not falling' brought the fox body and why 'not being blind' shed it, then calls the pair 'two throws, one game.' This occurrence anchors the paired formula cited in the prose.

Occurrences.Kwic: 豈可撥去不落，守箇不昧，無繩自縛？不見黃檗於不落不昧之後，問箇轉轉不錯，打丈一掌，深契百丈之意。豈不以明不昧因果，正三句一時說之旨麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chaozong (朝宗禪師語錄), spoken by Chaozong Tongren: he rebukes rejecting 'not falling' and clinging to 'not being blind' as tying oneself without a rope, then continues by affirming 'not being blind to cause and effect' in his stated frame.
